The cost is that a skeptical or specialist reader has to flip to the back to find out which studies you mean, and reviewers in some quarters will note the omission.

**Handling contested or failed replications.** Since the replication discussions of the last decade or so, it has become much more common to put the state of the evidence in the running text rather than burying it in a note — hedged reporting verbs for the original finding, then a plain statement of what happened when others tried to repeat it. Naming is specific and lets a reader follow the chain, but it picks a fight, dates the book, and some publishers get cautious about characterizing a named competitor's claims. Generalizing avoids all that, at the cost that a reader can't verify the comparison.
